name: Gareth Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential, so tell me what you would say at work and, separately, what you think privately. What happens on an ordinary day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Gareth, 27, and I lead the team maintaining scheduling software for a tech company. I have a master’s degree and a reputation for finding a fault before it makes warehouse staff work the wrong shift. I read incident logs, review code changes and call the client when an unusual roster rule appears. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer code I can trace from start to finish.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much room do you have if work changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent alone and earn more than most developers in this job. I have about eleven months of expenses saved because I kept living in the same small flat after my pay rose. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby, but I would rather not leave a team that knows how to check its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau is what happens when the sales story outruns the software. A routine helper might save time, but our clients still need someone who understands shift rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel vindicated for not changing my whole workflow. My job and pay look solid, and the eleven-month cushion means an ordinary mistake would not put me near the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reading incident logs and checking roster code by hand. I’d continue saving 600 each month from my current salary. In the first year I’d ask the team to record which repetitive checks actually save time before buying another tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I still have the usual pressure when a client needs an urgent fix, but I do not expect my work or income to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a mistake you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One client changes the night shift after a holiday every year, and the software missed it once. I keep the holiday night-shift rule on a paper card beside my screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a junior developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the junior developers to follow the shift from the first rule to the final roster. If a helper saves ten minutes, fine, but the customer has to sleep after we send the schedule.

say: I see **AI Plateau** as routine help while clients still need people who understand shifts.
I would measure **actual time saved** before buying another tool.
think: I feel **vindicated** for keeping a workflow I can trace.
My **job and pay** feel secure with eleven months of costs saved.
do: **Keep** checking incident logs and roster code by hand.
**Record** which routine checks a helper genuinely speeds up.
feel: **Calm** about my own income despite ordinary client pressure.
S0.quote: I keep the holiday night-shift rule on a paper card beside my screen.
fieldNote: His **paper reminder** reflects care with recurring shift rules, not a lack of software skill.
High pay, **eleven months saved** and many local openings make the mild world secure for him.

steps.text: Keep checking roster code and incident logs by hand
Save 600 each month from current developer pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will make management expect code and client replies much faster. I would ask for a proper trial before any target changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry my refusal to use AI tools will look like poor leadership. Even with good results, a cheaper team that uses them could replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our quality lead to run the approved assistant on last year’s wrong-shift incidents while I check the results. If it passes, I’d learn to use it on copied roster data, not live client schedules. In the first year I’d take the company’s paid course on shift-rule design if offered, and keep saving 600 while employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I may have almost a year of savings, but I could still lose a well-paid lead job if I refuse every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use to judge the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my manager the incident where the night shift doubled after a holiday. If the assistant misses it, I’d demand another test before a rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you learn the assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trial works, I would sit with the quality lead for a week and learn the approved tool. I would not quietly paste client rosters into a public chatbot.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to raise speed targets for code and client replies.
I would insist on a **proper trial** before those targets change.
think: I fear my **AI refusal** may make good results look like poor leadership.
I could lose my **lead job** to a cheaper tool-using team.
do: **Test** the approved assistant on old wrong-shift incidents with the quality lead.
**Learn** the approved tool on copied rosters if it passes the trial.
**Take** the paid shift-rule course if offered, and keep saving 600 monthly while employed.
feel: **Anxious** about losing a well-paid role despite substantial savings.
S1.quote: I could still lose a well-paid lead job if I refuse every new tool.
fieldNote: He is **resistant**, but a successful trial could bring a narrow, controlled first use.
His **strong buffer** softens a possible gap, not the risk of losing a high-paying role.

steps.text: Use the approved assistant on copied roster cases if the trial passes
Take the paid shift-rule design course if offered
Keep saving 600 monthly while employed during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 reaches our planning and code in 2028. Robots for hands-on warehouse work come around 2031, so our desk jobs do not get those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company could replace most scheduling code work and retain a small client team, if any. Eleven months saved is helpful, but nearby developer jobs could be shrinking at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d hold off on buying the small flat I have been looking at and keep my deposit liquid. I’d ask management for written severance and transition terms, then check actual client-support vacancies. In the first year after 2028, if I am laid off, I’d apply to existing openings and use the deposit for rent while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect a large cut in developer income, and even a long cushion has an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat purchase?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the estate agent to stop the flat search before I pay for inspections. A mortgage would turn a job shock into a debt problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written notice and paid time to search, but I would not assume the company grants either. If no support job exists, I would keep looking rather than call it a fallback.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach scheduling code before warehouse robots arrive.
I would ask for **written severance** and transition terms.
think: I expect a **large coding cut** and perhaps only a small client team.
My **eleven-month buffer** may outlast one gap but cannot guarantee another developer job.
do: **Postpone** buying a flat and keep the deposit liquid now.
**Request** written severance and transition terms from management.
**Apply** for actual client-support openings after 2028 if laid off.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected income loss despite nearly a year of savings.
S2.quote: A mortgage would turn a job shock into a debt problem.
fieldNote: He correctly faces the **2028 desk-work shock** before warehouse robots around 2031.
His **support search** depends on actual vacancies; he retains the flat deposit for rent instead of assuming a safe field.

steps.text: Postpone buying a flat and keep the deposit liquid
Apply for actual client-support vacancies if laid off after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to document every odd roster rule. Robots around 2034 reach the warehouse later, while our code faces thinking AI in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would still expect my code role to shrink, but I could test a move into quality work while earning my current salary. I would not call quality a safe refuge. A general system might test software too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one afternoon monthly with the quality lead learning how client faults are investigated. I’d take a certified quality course if my company pays; otherwise I’d use its free materials. In the first year after 2031, if my role is cut, I’d apply for real quality or client-support openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less hurried than in 2028. I could keep the flat deposit safe and learn enough to judge whether a different role really exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove you learned quality work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the holiday night-shift incident and ask the quality lead to grade my fault report. If I cannot explain the root cause, a certificate would be paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your flat deposit on training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the deposit in cash rather than pay tuition. The course needs employer funding or a real offer that requires it.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to document unusual roster rules.
I know **2034 robots** do not delay the 2031 code change.
think: I expect my **code role** to shrink despite the longer warning.
I cannot assume **quality work** survives full thinking AI either.
do: **Study** client-fault investigations with the quality lead monthly.
**Take** an employer-funded quality course, or use free company materials if funding fails.
**Apply** for real quality or support openings after 2031 if my role is cut.
feel: **Anxious** about work, with time to test a different path.
S3.quote: A general system might test software too.
fieldNote: He uses the **five-year window** to test a path, while recognizing quality roles may also be automated.
His **training decision** preserves the deposit unless employer funding or a real offer justifies tuition.

steps.text: Learn fault investigation monthly and take employer-funded training or free company materials
Apply for existing quality or support roles if laid off after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 offers a decade to change the work without rushing a poor tool into production. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2036; warehouse robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can build another line of technical skill in ten years, but I dislike being told to abandon reliable methods early. I expect my salary to hold for now, with plenty of firms still hiring nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading roster releases and have the quality lead check one investigation I write each quarter. I’d continue saving 600 monthly while my high pay holds and take a work-funded course once a year if offered. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare real offers and conditions before leaving this company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the decade ahead, but secure in my work and rent for the next few years. I have time to test each change instead of betting on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the flat during the longer runway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep renting until a purchase fits both my income and the changing work. I would not buy a flat simply because the deposit is sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another employer attractive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a firm nearby offered a quality role with clear pay and a tested workflow, I would consider it. I would keep my scheduling job until a nearby firm makes a real offer.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to test changes without rushing production.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect my **salary** to hold for now with many nearby firms hiring.
I resist abandoning **reliable methods** before a replacement proves itself.
do: **Keep** leading roster releases and checking one quality investigation quarterly.
**Take** a work-funded quality course yearly if offered.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term change, with secure work and rent now.
S4.quote: I would keep my scheduling job until a nearby firm makes a real offer.
fieldNote: His **strong savings** and many local jobs create room for cautious trials over a decade.
He makes **courses and moves** conditional on funding and real offers, not forecasts.

steps.text: Keep leading roster releases and reviewing quality investigations quarterly
Save 600 each month while developer pay remains high
Take a work-funded quality course yearly if offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I might have eleven months of expenses saved, but the other software jobs could vanish alongside mine. Written severance, paid search time and a truthful list of current vacancies would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the warehouse worker who gets the wrong roster. A scheduling error is not just a bad number on a screen; someone misses a shift and a wage.

headlineQuote: A scheduling error is not just a bad number on a screen; someone misses a shift and a wage.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old scheduling lead** with a master’s degree, high developer pay and about eleven months of expenses saved.
He has **never used AI** and trusts code he can trace, though a successful controlled trial could change his mind.
A **strong cushion** protects rent in mild change, but fast AGI could cut his own coding income.
He would **test tools cautiously**, seek funded quality training and apply only to real openings if his role ends.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his well-paid coding role while nearby developer jobs shrink too.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid search time and a truthful list of current vacancies would help.
